title: Three biggest concerns from Inter's ugly 4-3 Champions League loss vs. Club Brugge - CBS Sports
description: A leaky back line, costly goalkeeping mistakes and seven losses in eight European games show Cristian Chivu's squ
body:
A leaky back line, costly goalkeeping mistakes and seven losses in eight European games show Cristian Chivu's squad faces major structural issues that domestic form can no longer mask
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 13, 2026
                            
                    at
    6:40 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        MILAN -- If we look at the recent Champions League numbers, Inter are not a serious contender. The Nerazzurri have lost seven of their last eight European matches stretchning back to last season, and lost the opening two matches of the current league phase against Real Madrid and Club Brugge. While the opening defeat against Jose Mourinho's team showed some positive aspects, the second match was completely different. Inter were defeated 4-3 at San Siro on Tuesday, putting forward a crushingly bad defensive performance. Cristian Chivu's side looks dominant in Italy, but in Europe it is much different and they're going to need to change something over the remaining six matches of the league phase if they want to succeed or even simply repeat what they have done over the last several years, when they finished as runners up in two Champions League finals in three years from 2023 to 2025. Here's the four most worrying things that took place in Milan on Tuesday: 1. Defensive issues 
The defense is seriously becoming an issue for the Nerazzurri. Inter conceded six goals in the opening two Champions League games and eight in six Serie A matches for a total of 14 goals conceded in eight matches so far. Numbers that are not enough if Inter want to compete domestically and in Europe, considering the level of their rivals. While in the Italian league conceding goals don't mean losing games, as Inter are still undefeated thanks to some incredible comebacks against Napoli, Udinese and AS Roma, in Europe things are much more difficult. Apart from numbers, there are some players that are not at their best form up to now. One of them is Manuel Akanji who was signed permanently in the summer from Manchester City. After both Stefan de Vrij and Francesco Acerbi left the club in the summer 2026, he's the one leading the defense now, as John Stones is still recovering from a muscular injury. So far, he has yet to deliver the performances expected of him, and Inter's most recent goal conceded against Club Brugge exposed clear signs that the team is still short of its ideal physical condition. Clearly, Inter's defensive issues are not an issue of a single man, but there are some worrying signals coming from the most expert players. 2. Woeful goalkeeping 
For the second Champions League match in a row, an Inter goalkeeper made a costly mistake that led to Club Brugge scoring the second goal of the game, the one that basically changed the momentum of the game. Even if Josep Martinez made a few more saves that helped the Nerazzurri to avoid more goals conceded, this is a moment of reflection for Chivu as second goalkeeper Ivan Provedel is likely to have a chance in the next weeks to pick up some minutes through rotation. A mistake doesn't define a player, but this is the second one in less than a month. 
3. Lautaro's biggest mistake It's not just about defenders or the goalkeeper; Inter captain and striker Lautaro Martinez missed a key chance in the second half that was probably going to change the direction of the game. The Argentinian player missed a goal in front of his former goalkeeper and teammate Yann Sommer, who now plays for Club Brugge. More than a save, it was a mistake of Lautaro, who also scored two goals at San Siro but wasn't able to replicate the hat trick of his rival on Tuesday, Nicolò Tresoldi, the MVP of the night in Milan. The Italian striker, who currently represents Germany at Under-21 level, is expected to decide which national team to represent next summer, after the U21 European Championship. Italy may have found a striker to build its future around, or at least this is what Roberto Mancini is hoping for.

title: St. John's point guard Quinn Ellis cleared by NCAA: Ex-EuroLeague product poised to shine in Big East - CBS Sports
description: What to expect from the former EuroLeague point guard and how it affects St. John's outlook in 2026-27
body:
What to expect from the former EuroLeague point guard and how it affects St. John's outlook in 2026-27
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 13, 2026
                            
                    at
    4:13 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        St. John's point guard Quinn Ellis was ruled eligible Tuesday, one day before the Johnnies lace up against Drexel in the season's first exhibition. Ellis, 23, was one of the top targets in free agency after shining in the EuroLeague last season for Olimpia Milano. The 6-foot-4 guard profiles as a high-feel, steadying hand for a St. John's club that had to replace all five starters, including the irreplaceable Zuby Ejiofor. Ellis averaged 8.2 points, 4.3 rebounds and 4.5 assists with just 1.7 turnovers in 36 games competing in the second-best basketball league in the world. Rick Pitino has lofty expectations for Ellis, lumping him right next to Daniss Jenkins and Kadary Richmond — both All-Big East talents — as one of the most talented point guards he's coached at St. John's. With Ellis in the fold, St. John's is prepared to shift its offensive identity to a perimeter-focused attack. Instead of relying on Ejiofor, Bryce Hopkins and Dillon Mitchell to smash opponents into submission with physical drives and a boatload of offensive rebounds, Ellis gives St. John's a chance to be one of the better pick-and-roll offenses in the Big East, especially since he's paired with a knockdown shooter like Ian Jackson and an elite slasher like top-rated Baylor transfer Tounde Yessoufou.Ellis will be one of the highest-paid point guards in all of college basketball next season, but his eligibility had come into scrutiny after the NCAA introduced stricter eligibility guidelines for international prospects in late May … a month after St. John's had landed Ellis' commitment over a horde of other high-major schools. Make no mistake, Ellis was a full-blown professional basketball player. He signed a multi-year deal with Milano in July of 2025, but he was able to get cleared because he was still within his five-year window of graduating high school and had his transcripts in order. Since he is already 23 years old, Ellis will only have one more year of eligibility. Utah's Noam Yaacov (academics) and LSU's Yam Madar (not within the five-year eligibility clock window) are two high-profile examples of the NCAA axing potential international professionals from playing college basketball this season.While they play different positions, Ellis is in a similar boat as 23-year-old Virginia forward Thijs De Ridder, who played professionally in Belgium but was cleared by the NCAA this time last year because he was still within that five-year eligibility clock window. De Ridder went on to lead Virginia in scoring at 15.6 points per game and help flip UVa into a 30-win club. The bruising 4-man is a popular preseason ACC Player of the Year in 2026-27. 
St. John's is hoping for a similar cannonball into college hoops for Ellis, who should team up with Yessoufou and Jackson to give St. John's one of the Big East's most dynamic backcourts. That trio can go toe-to-toe with UConn's electric duo of Silas Demary Jr. and Braylon Mullins. If Pitino's Hall of Fame coaching can vault this new-look St. John's frontcourt into one of the better rebounding clubs in the Big East, the Johnnies could certainly be in the mix to make the Final Four with this high-ceiling backcourt at center stage of the pitch.
An eligible Ellis is a big deal, but Pitino's outfit is not quite out of the woods yet on the eligibility front. Auburn transfer Keyshawn Hall is still fighting for a fifth year of eligibility in the ongoing 5-for-5 case. He is currently eligible to suit up for the Johnnies thanks to a temporary restraining order, but that legal process is still ongoing. Forward Babacar Sane was ruled ineligible by the NCAA because he signed an Exhibit 10 deal with the Utah Jazz in June of 2024, but he never played in a game. Sane is appealing that ruling and has another court hearing scheduled for Nov. 9.St. John's will play Monmouth in the season-opener on Nov. 2.

title: Payton Pritchard contract: Why two-year, $44 million deal is bargain for Celtics - CBS Sports

body:
With an NBA championship and Sixth Man of the Year Award already under his belt, Pritchard is set for an even bigger role in Boston this season
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 13, 2026
                            
                    at
    5:07 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Upward mobility in the NBA contractual market is pretty rare. A player's financial destiny is often tied to where he is drafted. Where that player is drafted frequently determines the opportunities he gets early in his career, which in turn determines his rookie extension, what he's eligible for on his next deal and so on. One team-friendly contract tends to beget several, and nowhere is that truer right now than it is for Payton Pritchard.On Tuesday, he and the Boston Celtics agreed to a two-year, $44.2 million contract extension, according to ESPN. All told, that will guarantee him around $85 million in NBA earnings through the first 10 seasons of his career. That is by no means a bad outcome, on paper, for the No. 26 pick in the 2020 NBA Draft. Just consider it in comparison to the No. 4 pick, Patrick Williams, who has locked in over $130 million in career earnings thus far.Williams has, at no point, been a better NBA player than Pritchard. He is now a fringe rotation player for the Chicago Bulls, a lottery team. But he was a high draft pick with great physical tools that tend to get players paid. He played for a Chicago team that, through its own poor management, had few other players worth paying, so the Bulls were free to give him a bloated contract, betting on improvement that hasn't really come.
Pritchard has dealt under almost the exact opposite circumstances. He landed on a loaded Celtics team that couldn't find him consistent minutes. Things got bad enough around the 2023 trade deadline that Pritchard reportedly wanted to be dealt. Without much of a resume after three years, the Celtics locked him into a four-year, $30 million rookie extension that guaranteed him life-changing wealth, but still represented a pittance compared to what he was actually worth. He won Sixth Man of the Year and a championship before that extension even kicked in.
Normally, a standard veteran extension can give a player a 40% raise in the final season of their current deal. This is why those early contracts matter. If a team believes in you when you're young, it makes you eligible to extend for more when you get older. Yet Pritchard's deal is so low that he's actually capped at a different figure: 140% of the estimated average player salary in the first year of his extension. He could therefore only extend for around $67 million over three years. He wound up taking the shorter, two-year equivalent of that deal with a mutual option that gives the sides flexibility to tear up the contract and renegotiate something a bit bigger in the 2029 offseason.That deal, by most analytical measures, is a pretty significant bargain. Could Pritchard be even better in an increased role?Stephen Noh of Sporting News built a tool that determines a player's projected value using the DPM all-in-one metric. It projects Pritchard to be worth around $28 million next year and going forward. This deal keeps him in Boston for an average of $22 million per year.These projections are based on who Pritchard has already been. It's worth wondering, now that Jaylen Brown has been traded, who Pritchard might soon become. As Yahoo's Tom Haberstroh noted after the Brown trade, Pritchard's usage rate went up nearly nine percentage points when he played without Brown a year ago... and his true shooting improved by four percentage points in those minutes. The Celtics went 32-5 in games in which Pritchard's usage reached or exceeded 22% last season.
Pritchard has never been a full-time starter. There's a chance he will be this season, and if he is, he's suddenly on a roster equipped to give him shots and minutes he's never had before. Some, like Haberstroh, have even suggested he's primed for a Jalen Brunson-esque leap as a small guard finally being given the freedom to spread his wings. While such notions are probably a bit optimistic, it's not unreasonable to believe Pritchard is headed for his most productive NBA season.And if he is, the Celtics will still have three years of cost control on a severely undervalued player through this extension. If they elect to renegotiate his deal through the mutual option in 2029, they'll have the leverage to yet again do so in a team-friendly manner. After all, mutual options require both parties to opt out. If the Celtics simply want Pritchard to play out the 2029-30 season on this deal, they can make him do so.Every team in the NBA would rather have high picks than lower ones. The top of the draft is typically where superstars are found, and even if those superstars cost more, they're a prerequisite for championship contention. The Celtics know that. Look at all of the success they had with Brown and Jayson Tatum.
But the Pritchard contract is an example of just how much surplus value nailing a pick later on in the draft can generate. Those are the players who tend to be undervalued on their second contract, which trickles down to their third and fourth deals as well. In an NBA increasingly obsessed with maximizing every last cent, success stories like Boston's with Pritchard are becoming nearly as essential to genuine championship contention as landing stars always have been.

        It may be partially the product of having four teams on a bye, or all the injuries at the wide receiver position, but one thing you'll notice when looking at this week's Fantasy Football wide receiver rankings is that good things come in twos. In our consensus rankings, there are two Cowboys in the top 12, but we always expected CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens to be that good. It's also not surprising to see Puka Nacua and Davante Adams in the top 16, especially when you consider they are playing the Cardinals. But what about two Packers, Christian Watson and Matthew Golden, in the top 14? Or two Panthers, Tetairoa McMillan and Jalen Coker, in the top 18? Or two Saints, Chris Olave and Devaughn Vele, in the top 24? That's right, 10 of our top 24 receivers this week come from five teams. That's shocking. What's more shocking is that the Steelers almost made it six.Even after his disappointing Week 5, DK Metcalf comes in at WR21 in our consensus rankings and he is ranked top 25 in all three experts' rankings. You might think that's because Michael Pittman and Roman Wilson are out, but if you scroll down just a bit further, you see the top waiver wire receiver, Germie Bernard, ranked at WR27. What in the world?Bernard did catch six of nine targets for 80 yards in Week 5, so this isn't coming out of nowhere. But how can we be so confident in two receivers for Aaron Rodgers? Credit Mike McCarthy. Rodgers is averaging 36.8 passes per game and eight air yards per attempt. His 65.5% true dropback rate is his highest in the last five years and more of those targets are going to receivers than they did last year. Rodgers isn't his old self, not by any stretch, but the combination of volume and downfield targets has made his receivers more viable than they've been in a while. Which is why we think you can not only add Bernard this week, but start him as a high-end WR3.Here is the rest of the Week 6 WR preview:

title: Could Man City lose 2023 UCL crown as they await appeal and potential PL punishments? - CBS Sports
description: The Citizens will play their first home game since the charges as potentially massive punishments could come thei
body:
The Citizens will play their first home game since the charges as potentially massive punishments could come their way
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 13, 2026
                            
                    at
    5:45 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            6 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Manchester City will face PSG on Wednesday at the Etihad Stadium for the second matchday of their Champions League campaign and the game against the French giants is a really ironic coincidence. Wednesday's clash will be the first home game played by the team led by Enzo Maresca after an independent commission upheld 114 of 115 charges brought by the Premier League in relation to City's violations of the competition's financial rules, and it will take place against PSG, another big European team that had to face similar issues in the past. The Citizens are dealing with the most challenging moment of their recent history, as the club are appealing and have maintained their innocence as they and the rest of the league await news of a sanction that could deepen the crisis for the eight-time English champions and the English game as a whole. The match at the Etihad follows the heated away game against Liverpool that took place on Sunday, when the home crowd protested Maresca's team before and during the game. However, Erling Haaland and his teammates reacted on the field and delivered a strong performance, winning 3-0 at Anfield. The home fans are expected to support the club and the ownership, as they also did it when traveling on Sunday at Liverpool and will also be joined by former team manager Pep Guardiola, who will make his first comeback at the Etihad for the first time since he left the club in the summer, when he was replaced by Maresca. Earlier this month, Guardiola wrote in a social media post, "I want every single Manchester City fan across the world to know I am here; more than ever. I am, always have been, always will, be behind my club, my owner, my chairman, Ferran [Soriano], the players, staff, [manager] Enzo [Maresca] and you, our unique supporters. Let me be clear: we will get through this together. I love you all."Guardiola was the manager of Manchester City from 2016 to 2026, winning also the 2023 edition of the UEFA Champions League, the first one won by the club. In recent days, following the publication of the independent commission's verdict, questions have emerged over whether Manchester City could be stripped of their Champions League title. Speculation has also mounted over the possibility of the club losing domestic honors, including Premier League titles. However, as things stand, there is no indication that City's 2023 European crown is under threat. 
Here's why. What happens to the 2023 title? Manchester City are appealing against the decision of the Premier League's independent commission investigation which determined that between the 2009-10 season and the 2017-18 season, City breached spending limits, had "sham" contracts, misstated their accounts, and did other things to make it seem as if their revenue was in line with Premier League spending limits. UEFA, the European governing body, didn't open a new procedure against Manchester City following the recent events, but sources told Sky Sport UK that "UEFA is monitoring developments and will wait until the end of the Premier League's disciplinary process before deciding whether to take any potential action against Manchester City."From 2009 to 2018, Manchester City were found to have broken the Premier League's financial rules, including five charges of failing to comply with UEFA's Financial Fair Play rules (FFP). At the time of the breaches, FFP rules required clubs to operate within set break-even limits, meaning their spending had to be broadly in line with their football-related revenues.UEFA have previously sanctioned Manchester City for breaking the FFP rules. In 2014, the English club entered into a settlement agreement with the European body which included a $60 million fine, but were told they would get €40 million back if they stuck to the terms of their settlement. In 2020, City were again found guilty of breaking the FFP rules, and were fined $30 million and banned from playing European tournaments for two years. However, the club appealed to the CAS (Court of Arbitration for Sports) which ruled that UEFA didn't establish that City owners had "disguised equity funding as sponsorship contributions," and CAS reduced the fine from $30 million to $10 million for failing to co-operate with the UEFA investigation and wrote in a statement that the alleged breaches "were either not established or time-barred". City were not ultimately banned from European tournaments.
UEFA has a statute of limitations of five years for financial rule breaches, while the Premier League does not and this is why it's too early to say if there will be sanctions imposed on the club by UEFA in the future, and this is why their 2023 Champions League title shouldn't be considered in doubt, at least for now. The surreal scenario Technically, Manchester City could play in both the second division and in Champions League next season, in case they are relegated from the Premier League. According to the BBC, Manchester City's current situation should not affect their UEFA licence, which is required for clubs to compete in European competitions. UEFA could still launch disciplinary proceedings in the future, but that alone would not necessarily put the club's licence at risk. Speaking to the BBC, one source said that City's licence "had been raised" and that a solution "would require the sort of joined-up thinking that's been a bit lacking so far."Licenses are issued by the Football Association while the process is delegated to the Premier League and they are based on current financial books but don't consider sanctions or breaches from the past. This is why, in case of a relegation, Manchester City would potentially be able to play European soccer. 
Why can't City appeal to CAS now? CAS, the legal body that settles sports disputes, can't handle the Manchester City case at this stage. They cover 900 cases per year, covering more than 50 sports, and they is based in Switzerland. As mentioned above, Manchester City already appealed to CAS in 2020 and partially won the case, as CAS overturned the decision of UEFA to ban the English club for two years. In accordance with English law, the agreement made by the Premier League teams states that all the cases involving English clubs are conducted in England and Wales, meaning the Swiss legal body can't operate in such territory. How PSG handled it PSG, the rivals of Manchester City on Wednesday, also had to face similar issues with UEFA in the past. It all started in 2018 when the German magazine Der Spiegel published the "Football Leaks" scandal claimed that between them Qatar and Abu Dhabi have injected $5.1 billion to increase the budgets of the clubs they own. According to the information at the time, PSG agreed on a five-year deal with the Qatar Tourism Authority (QTA), worth €1.075 billion, or €215 million a year and the "overestimated" sponsorship deals of Manchester City with the Abu Dhabi owners. Both clubs have signed settlement agreements with UEFA and PSG were fined €10 million by UEFA in 2022 for not complying with financial rules since 2018, with another €50 million fine suspended.According to the "Football Leaks" documents in 2018, current FIFA president Gianni Infantino, who was the UEFA general secretary back at the time, had a key role in avoiding serious sanctions in 2014 and personally met with officials of both clubs for "secret talks, even supplying them with confidential materials that involved suggested compromises that he was unauthorized to propose."
Nasser Al-Khelaifi, president of Qatar-owned Paris Saint-Germain since 2011, currently heads the European Club Association (ECA). He took over the role in 2021, following the departure of former president Andrea Agnelli, then Juventus chairman, who stepped down amid the fallout from the European Super League project, which he had helped launch earlier that year. PSG are now in a different position from Manchester City, also because the French Ligue 1 didn't have the same approach as the Premier League. The two sides meet at the Etihad on Wednesday in what promises to be one of the best fixtures of the week. Yet beyond the action on the pitch, the political battles and behind-the-scenes power struggles that have shaped European soccer over the past decade remain an equally important part of the story that shouldn't be forgotten.

        Despite his ongoing struggles, Shohei Ohtani will be in the Game 3 starting lineup for the Los Angeles Dodgers on Wednesday in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series against the Milwaukee Brewers, manager Dave Roberts announced Tuesday."He's adamant he feels good enough to be in there. He's close to finding something with his swing. I feel great about it," Roberts said Tuesday. "He wants to be in there and help us win a ballgame and win a championship. Great conversation, and I'm excited about having him in there." Ohtani, who is nursing knee and biceps injuries, is 3 for 20 this postseason and 11 for 70 (.157) with zero home runs in his last 24 games dating back to August 18. He spent 12 days on the injured list in September and has just one hit in eight NLCS plate appearances as the Dodgers have fallen behind 2-0 in the best-of-seven series. "The results, I take full responsibility," Ohtani said through an interpreter Tuesday. "That's all I can really say, why the results haven't been where I wanted it to be. I think there's different approaches to this, whether that be focusing on reducing the symptoms and getting rid of the pain and/or just making sure that I'm moving well in the swing." 

        
            
                Would the Dodgers actually bench Shohei Ohtani? Struggling superstar faces questions amid 2-0 NLCS hole
                
                    Dayn Perry                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
Following the Game 2 loss on Monday, Roberts said the Dodgers would have a "conversation" about Ohtani's place in the lineup. He is clearly not himself at the plate. His swings are off-balance and his contact quality is way down. Simply put, Ohtani looks like an injured player -- one who is not capable of helping his team score runs or win games at the moment."The symptoms have subdued a lot," Ohtani said. "Especially when I was on the IL, spending that time just being able to reduce the symptoms.  As of now with the swing, it's a daily process of trying different things, different feel on a daily basis."  The Dodgers have a very good DH alternative in top prospect Josue De Paula. De Paula, 21, reached base 21 times in 11 regular-season games and has pinch-hit three times in key spots this postseason, and worked two walks. Los Angeles has nine singles and one double in the two NLCS losses to the Brewers. Their offense is lacking.
"We remember vividly at this time last year that he maybe had the best baseball game ever played the day he pitched against us and hit a home run every time up, it seemed like," Brewers manager Pat Murphy said Wednesday when asked about Ohtani's struggles at the plate. "You can't forget that, his capabilities."Now 32, Ohtani hit .275/.377/.512 with 30 home runs during the regular season, which would be a career year for most players but is a down year for Ohtani. He threw 85 ⅔ innings with a 1.79 ERA before the injuries. Ohtani has not pitched since July 3 and won't return to the mound this postseason.Teams with a 2-0 lead in a best-of-seven series have historically gone on to win the series 83% of the time.         Atlanta Dream star Allisha Gray underwent a "minor" procedure on her left shooting hand to address an injury she sustained during the semifinals against the New York Liberty. It's unclear when the procedure took place, and her status for Game 1 of the 2026 WNBA Finals against the Golden State Valkyries on Saturday is still up in the air. "Right now I'm day-to-day, I had a minor procedure," Gray said Tuesday in an interview with WSB-TV. "Progress is great, so as of right now I'm just day-to-day, and you'll see."Gray, whose 19 points per game in the regular season led the Dream and ranked ninth in the league, was injured early in Game 1 against the Liberty when she deflected a pass from Sabrina Ionescu. After a short trip to the locker room, Gray returned to the game with tape on her fingers. Her first shot was a bad miss from 3-point range, so she removed the tape. In the second quarter, she made another nice defensive play on Ionescu, but aggravated the injury in the process and has not played since. 
Despite Gray's absence, the Dream swept the Liberty in three games to advance to the WNBA Finals. Gray was on the court Tuesday, taking part in shooting drills during the portion of the Dream's practice that was open to the media. She had her left ring and pinky fingers taped together. 
Dream's title chances may hinge on Gray's availability"Allisha's one of the best players in the W," Dream coach Karl Smesko said Tuesday. "To advance and beat a great New York team basically without her, except for 10 minutes of one game, is a testament to everybody else raising their game. But it would be great to have her back for the Finals. She's just somebody that, offensively, is really hard to stop, and then she makes defensive plays. She's just an all-around great player."

The Dream's ability to beat the Valkyries and win the first championship in franchise history may hinge on Gray's availability. Jordin Canada, DeWanna Bonner and Isobel Borlase were spectacular in the semifinals against the Liberty, but it's a big ask for them to repeat these performances:Canada had three of the five-highest playoff scoring performances of her career against the Liberty, and averaged 22.3 points on 62.2/61.5/100 shooting splits -- up from 11.6 points on 43.1/29.2/78.2 shooting in the regular season. Bonner went for 15.3 points and 8.3 rebounds on 50/46.7/80 shooting splits, up from 10.4 points and six rebounds on 40.2/27.9/84.3 shooting between the Phoenix Mercury and Dream in the regular season. And Borlase, who only had six double-digit scoring games in the regular season, came off the bench to chip in 11 points in Game 2 and 10 points in Game 3 while shooting 9 of 15, including 3 of 6 from 3-point range. The Valkyries have the best defense in the league by a wide margin, and just shut down A'ja Wilson and Jackie Young in a sweep of the Las Vegas Aces. Ashley Sanchez and Mallory Swanson scored to help the U.S. team claw their way out of a 2-0 deficit against the world champions

        CHESTER, Pa. – The U.S. women's national team needed to start solidly against Spain on Tuesday, four days after the visitors took a two-goal lead in 14 minutes and never looked back. The steady start came but by the 32nd minute, the USWNT were in the same exact pickle. Two defensive lapses cost them against the reigning world champions and the USWNT were in need of a problem-solver with roughly an hour still left on the clock.On a team that boasts several likely suspects, one finally emerged – Ashley Sanchez.
Sophia Wilson darted towards goal but with a defender inching closer, she sent the ball to her left. It slowly drifted towards Sanchez, who had the space to do whatever she wanted. She cut inside and entered the penalty area, unbothered by the two defenders in front of her who had otherwise proven to be up for the task of handling the U.S. team's historically capable offense. They left a crevice of space that only the most talented of players could exploit, Sanchez rising to the challenge effortlessly. The ball took a bounce near the goal line but she took the hit for a reason – no one was in a position to stop it and so it landed in the back of the net, just as she had intended.The moment of brilliance is hardly a surprise from the NWSL's golden boot leader, the 27-year-old in the form of her life and as well-equipped as any to rattle an otherwise sturdy Spain back line. Sanchez had earned her spot in the starting lineup on Tuesday, the USWNT's most dynamic attacker a natural inclusion on a day they hoped to show the attacking end product that was missing in Saturday's loss. The overall results were mixed – the U.S. team still came out with a 2-2 draw, Spain the aggressors this time on a day where their attacking might was genuinely hard to miss. In Sanchez, though, the USWNT had a bright spot.
Until Sanchez's goal, the USWNT had gone goalless in 139 minutes of play against Spain and not for a lack of effort. Finishing was an issue – they generated 2.26 expected goals without actually scoring, the issue exemplified in Lily Yohannes' missed penalty midway through the second half. Matters felt worse at halftime of Tuesday's defeat, the U.S. team only generating 0.23 expected goals from six shots. They were in desperate need of someone who would finally make a difference and Sanchez stepped up, both at a timely juncture for the team and for herself.Sanchez had been out of the national team picture for two years until this month's friendlies, though her return had become undeniable by the time Hayes named the roster two weeks earlier. She had pulled off the feat after a position change at the North Carolina Courage, enjoying the best season of her career as a left winger after years of playing in midfield. Finding a way to impress against Spain would be another challenge entirely but one Sanchez ultimately embraced, making her case not a moment too soon.The Spain friendlies were always destined to test the USWNT's depth, especially without a few key players through injury, Sanchez adding to the narrative in all the right ways. She started in the place of Alyssa Thompson, who was amongst the positives on Saturday and still very much looks like a potential starter at the Women's World Cup in eight months' time. That spot on the left of Hayes' preferred three-person front line, though, is as competitive as any on a team that has aimed to have cover in just about every position on the pitch.
Hayes has a good type of problem on her hands in that position, if this week's games are anything to go by. How she picks between two talented players who seem poised to make a difference on good days and bad is one of the many questions that await over the next eight months, though in some ways it may not need answering. On days where the U.S. team's shortcomings are on display, particularly in defense without the injured Naomi Girma and Sam Coffey, that very specific type of depth might be the exact thing to bail Hayes' side out of trouble in a make-or-break situation.

title: Rams' Alaric Jackson suspended for punching Bills' Bradley Chubb - CBS Sports

body:
Alaric Jackson hit the Bills' pass-rusher with an apparent sucker-punch following Buffalo's wild Monday night win
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 13, 2026
                            
                    at
    7:08 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        The Buffalo Bills picked up one of the wildest wins of the season on Monday night with an overtime victory over the Los Angeles Rams, and somehow, things actually got even wilder after the game. Rams left tackle Alaric Jackson threw a punch at Bills edge rusher Bradley Chubb and appeared to make contact with his face.The NFL suspended Jackson two games for the incident. He will be eligible to return to the active roster on Monday, Oct. 26, which sets him up to miss the Week 6 matchup with the Arizona Cardinals and Week 7 contest against the Las Vegas Raiders. His first game back from suspension will be on Nov. 1 against the Los Angeles Chargers.Following Buffalo's 37-34 win, several players from both teams stayed on the field to do a jersey exchange and that's when the drama started. Jackson was trading his jersey with Buffalo's Deone Walker and while that exchange was going on, Chubb was talking trash to Jackson. The Rams offensive lineman clearly didn't like what Chubb had to say because he walked straight over to the Bills' pass-rusher and got in his face. Jackson and Chubb then started yelling at each other, and that's when things got ugly.
At that point, the two players had to be separated by their teammates. You can see a video of the incident below. 
"After the game, as players were shaking hands and exchanging jerseys, Jackson struck Buffalo linebacker Bradley Chubb in the face after a brief confrontation, violating Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1, which applies to 'any act which is contrary to the generally understood principles of sportsmanship,'" the NFL said in a statement.As you can see, Jackson's punch was pretty blatant, and the suspension is unsurprising given the historical precedent for that punishment.
During the 2025 season, Lions safety Brian Branch got hit with a one-game suspension for instigating a post-game fight following a loss to the Chiefs. That altercation actually took place on Oct. 12, 2025, exactly one year before Jackson's punch. Jackson was suspended for two games in 2024 for violating the NFL's personal conduct policy, so this is not his first time standing under the league's watchful eye.Based on post-game video, it appears that Chubb was talking trash to anyone and everyone. 
After he left the field, Chubb was asked about the altercation. "Just emotions. You know what I mean," Chubb said of what happened, via the California Post. "Emotional game. It was a close game."In the video, you can see that Chubb put his hand in Jackson's face just before Jackson threw the punch and that may have instigated the situation. "They always catch the second guy, so I let him swing and my teammates held me back, so I just chilled," Chubb said. 
Bradley Chubb put his hand in Alaric Jackson's face before Jackson punched the Bills' defender.  
                                                                    NFL/ESPN
                                                            Chubb was also asked if he was quarreling with anyone specifically and it appears that Jackson wasn't the only Rams player he was talking trash to. "It was just the whole team," Chubb said. Chubb finished the game with just two tackles, but his team won and that's what matters.
